claims.claim: The plasticity was bidirectional between the proximal and distal axonal compartments following appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Thus, the plasticity was bidirectional between the proximal and distal axonal compartments.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that γ1-γ3 showed increased CS+:CS- while γ5 showed decreased CS+:CS-, representing opposite directions of plasticity.

claims.claim: Synaptic depression is the main described plasticity mechanism at the KC-MBON synapses following olfactory conditioning.
claims.source: Yet synaptic depression is the main described plasticity mechanism at the KC-MBON synapses following olfactory conditioning (Barnstedt et al., 2016; Modi et al., 2020; Owald et al., 2015; Perisse et al., 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Zhang and Roman, 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: In the γ1 compartment, aversive reinforcement via dopaminergic neuron stimulation produces synaptic depression.
claims.source: In the γ1 compartment, where it has been examined in detail with electrophysiology, aversive reinforcement via dopaminergic neuron stimulation produces synaptic depression (Hige et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hige et al., 2015a.

claims.claim: Following aversive conditioning, there was a reduction in the CS+ response relative to the CS- in the γ2 and γ3 compartments.
claims.source: Following aversive conditioning, there was a reduction in the CS+ response relative to the CS- in the γ2 and γ3 compartments (Figure 2C-H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 2G and H show statistically significant reductions in CS+ relative to CS- in γ2 and γ3 compartments.

claims.claim: The reduction in CS+ response in γ2 and γ3 following aversive conditioning was due to depression in the CS+ response.
claims.source: This was due to depression in the CS+ response, as the Δ(post/pre) of the CS+ was significantly lower than the odor-only controls in each compartment (Figure 2G and H).
claims.evidence: Figure 2G and H show the CS+ Δ(post/pre) was significantly lower than odor-only controls in both γ2 and γ3.

claims.claim: The γ4 and γ5 compartments exhibited no significant change in ACh release following aversive conditioning.
claims.source: The γ4 and γ5 compartments exhibited no significant change in ACh release (Figure 2I, J and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 2I and J show no statistically significant differences in any comparisons for γ4 and γ5 compartments.

claims.claim: Appetitive and aversive conditioning produced plasticity in the opposite direction in the γ2 and γ3 compartments.
claims.source: When compared to appetitive conditioning, aversive conditioning produced plasticity in the opposite direction in the γ2 and γ3 compartments (Figures 1L and 2K).
claims.evidence: Comparing Figure 1L (appetitive) and Figure 2K (aversive) shows opposite patterns of plasticity in γ2 and γ3 compartments.

claims.claim: Appetitive and aversive conditioning produced bidirectional plasticity within multiple compartments.
claims.source: Thus, appetitive and aversive conditioning produced bidirectional plasticity within multiple compartments, which likely represents a presynaptic contribution to learning-induced changes in odor responsivity among postsynaptic MBONs following conditioning (Berry et al., 2018; Hige et al., 2015a; Owald et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the opposite patterns of plasticity observed in the same compartments following appetitive versus aversive conditioning, with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Major sources of stimulus-evoked intracellular Ca2+ include influx through voltage-sensitive CaV2 channels.
claims.source: Major sources of stimulus-evoked intracellular Ca2+ include influx through voltage-sensitive CaV2 channels, which are involved in presynaptic short-term and homeostatic plasticity (Frank et al., 2006; Inchauspe et al., 2004; Ishikawa et al., 2005; Müller and Davis, 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Conditional Cac knockdown reduced Cac levels approximately 29%.
claims.source: Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis of Cac knockdown (driven ubiquitously with tubulin-Gal4) showed that conditional expression with this induction protocol reduced Cac levels ~29% (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1C shows qPCR data quantifying the reduction in Cac expression.

claims.claim: Control flies exhibited plasticity across the γ lobe in similar spatial patterns as observed in wild-type animals following appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Control flies (containing R13F02-Gal4, UAS-GRAB-ACh, and tub-Gal80ts, but lacking a UAS-RNAi) exhibited plasticity across the γ lobe in similar spatial patterns as observed in wild-type animals (↑CS+:CS- in γ1–3 and ↓CS+:CS- in γ5): there was a robust increase in the CS+:CS- and CS+ potentiation in γ1, with a strong trend toward an increase in CS+:CS- in γ2 (p = 0.052), an increase in the CS+ response in γ3, and a trend toward a CS+ decrease in γ5 (p = 0.120) (Figure 3C, E, F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 3F shows the plasticity patterns in control animals across all γ compartments.

claims.claim: When Cac was knocked down conditionally, odor-evoked ACh release was still observed.
claims.source: When Cac was knocked down conditionally, odor-evoked ACh release was still observed, demonstrating that synaptic exocytosis remained intact.
claims.evidence: This is stated in the text and can be inferred from Figure 3D and G showing ACh responses in Cac knockdown animals.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Cac eliminated CS+ potentiation across the γ1–γ3 compartments.
claims.source: Yet the CS+ potentiation was lost across the γ1–γ3 compartments (Figure 3D, E, G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 3G shows loss of significant CS+ potentiation in γ1-γ3 compartments when Cac is knocked down.

claims.claim: The presynaptic CaV2.1 channel is necessary for potentiation of ACh release induced by learning.
claims.source: This demonstrates that the presynaptic CaV2.1 channel is necessary for potentiation of ACh release induced by learning.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the loss of CS+ potentiation when Cac is knocked down (Figure 3).

claims.claim: The trend toward CS+ depression in the most distal γ5 compartment remained intact when Cac was knocked down.
claims.source: Interestingly, the trend toward CS+ depression in the most distal γ5 compartment remained intact when Cac was knocked down (Figure 3G and J).
claims.evidence: Figure 3G shows a trend (p=0.077) toward CS+ depression in γ5 even with Cac knockdown.

claims.claim: While presynaptic potentiation requires Cac across the MB compartments, depression may not.
claims.source: This suggests that while presynaptic potentiation requires Cac across the MB compartments, depression may not.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CS+ potentiation was lost with Cac knockdown but CS+ depression trends remained.

claims.claim: Control flies for conditional Cac knockdown experiments exhibited CS+ depression in the proximal γ2 and γ3 compartments following aversive conditioning.
claims.source: Control flies for conditional Cac knockdown experiments exhibited similar CS+ depression in the proximal γ2 and γ3 compartments following aversive conditioning (Figure 4A-C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4B shows significant CS+ depression in γ2 and γ3 compartments in control animals.

claims.claim: Knockdown of Cac did not appreciably impair depression of CS+ responses following aversive conditioning.
claims.source: Knockdown of Cac did not appreciably impair depression of CS+ responses (Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4E shows significant CS+ depression in γ2 even with Cac knockdown, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 shows similar patterns in other compartments.

claims.claim: Moderate knockdown of Cac does not affect learning-induced depression of ACh release.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that moderate knockdown of Cac does not affect learning-induced depression of ACh release (in contrast to potentiation).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the persistence of CS+ depression following aversive conditioning in Cac knockdown animals (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Conditional Cac knockdown impaired behavioral performance in appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Conditional Cac knockdown impaired behavioral performance (Figure 3H), reminiscent of its previously reported role in aversive conditioning (Hidalgo et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Figure 3H shows statistically significant reduction in performance index with Cac knockdown compared to controls.

claims.claim: Odor avoidance was unaffected by Cac knockdown.
claims.source: Odor avoidance was unaffected by Cac knockdown (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B), demonstrating that the effect was not due to loss of olfactory acuity.
claims.evidence: Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B shows no significant difference in odor avoidance between Cac knockdown and control animals.

claims.claim: Learning-induced facilitation of neurotransmitter release in the proximal γ compartments contributes to behavioral action selection in reward learning.
claims.source: Overall, these findings suggest that the learning-induced facilitation of neurotransmitter release in the proximal γ compartments contributes to behavioral action selection in reward learning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the combination of impaired CS+ potentiation (Figure 3G) and impaired behavioral learning (Figure 3H) when Cac is knocked down.

claims.claim: Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a major source of stimulus-evoked Ca2+ in neurons, including KCs.
claims.source: Ca2+ release from the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a major source of stimulus-evoked Ca2+ in neurons, including KCs, and modulates various forms of synaptic/homeostatic plasticity (Handler et al., 2019; James et al., 2019; Taufiq et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Knockdown of IP3R eliminated the post-conditioning contrast between the CS+ and CS-.
claims.source: Knockdown of IP3R eliminated the post-conditioning contrast between the CS+ and CS- (i.e. the difference between the CS+ and CS-) (Figure 4G-I, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4H shows no significant difference between CS+ and CS- Δ(post/pre) values when IP3R is knocked down.

claims.claim: Loss of post-conditioning contrast with IP3R knockdown was not due to a loss of depression in the CS+ groups, but rather due to the appearance of olfactory adaptation in the other groups.
claims.source: However, this was not due to a loss of depression in the CS+ groups, rather it was due to the appearance of olfactory adaptation in the other groups.
claims.evidence: Figure 4G and H show that CS- and odor-only controls exhibited decreased responses (Δ(post/pre) < 1) while CS+ depression remained.

claims.claim: In normal conditions, release of Ca2+ from the ER via IP3R is necessary to maintain odor responsivity upon repeated odor presentations.
claims.source: Therefore, in normal conditions, release of Ca2+ from the ER via IP3R is necessary to maintain odor responsivity upon repeated odor presentations.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the observation that IP3R knockdown led to adaptation in CS- and odor-only controls (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Loss of IP3R renders the KCs more susceptible to adaptation.
claims.source: Loss of IP3R renders the KCs more susceptible to adaptation at this time point (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 4H), reducing the contrast between the CS+ (which exhibits depression following aversive learning) and the other odor(s).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the increased adaptation observed in IP3R knockdown animals compared to controls.

claims.claim: Control animals exhibited no significant olfactory adaptation across 10 trials in any compartment.
claims.source: Control animals exhibited no significant olfactory adaptation across the 10 trials in any compartment (Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4K and Figure 4—figure supplement 2 show no statistically significant decreases in odor responses across trials in control animals.

claims.claim: Knocking down IP3R in KCs produced significant olfactory adaptation in the γ2 and γ3 compartments.
claims.source: In contrast, knocking down IP3R in KCs produced significant olfactory adaptation in the γ2 and γ3 compartments (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4L shows statistically significant decreases in odor-evoked ACh release across repeated presentations in γ2 with IP3R knockdown.

claims.claim: In γ2, following the fourth-odor presentation, there was a significant depression in odor-evoked ACh release at all-time points save one with IP3R knockdown.
claims.source: In γ2, following the fourth-odor presentation, there was a significant depression in odor-evoked ACh release at all-time points save one (Figure 4L, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 4L shows multiple time points with statistically significant decreases in ACh release in γ2 with IP3R knockdown.

claims.claim: The γ3 compartment showed significant depression in ACh release following the third-odor presentation with IP3R knockdown.
claims.source: A similar effect was observed in the γ3, where following the third-odor presentation, a significant depression in release occurred (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows statistically significant decreases in ACh release in γ3 with IP3R knockdown.

claims.claim: The γ1 compartment showed no evidence of adaptation with IP3R knockdown.
claims.source: The γ1 compartment showed no evidence of adaptation, suggesting that IP3R may support plasticity in this compartment via another mechanism (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows no statistically significant changes in γ1 with IP3R knockdown.

claims.claim: The γ4 and γ5 compartments exhibited no significant adaptation with IP3R knockdown.
claims.source: The γ4 and γ5 compartments exhibited no significant adaptation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 2 shows no statistically significant changes in γ4 and γ5 with IP3R knockdown.

claims.claim: IP3R-dependent Ca2+ release from the ER may contribute to maintenance of synaptic strength, preventing adaptation during repeated stimuli.
claims.source: Overall, these data suggest that IP3R-dependent Ca2+ release from the ER may contribute to maintenance of synaptic strength, preventing adaptation during repeated stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the observation that IP3R knockdown leads to adaptation across repeated odor presentations (Figure 4).

claims.claim: Loss of IP3R leads to alterations in neurotransmitter release that particularly impact compartments dominated by CS+ depression.
claims.source: Further, loss of IP3R leads to alterations in neurotransmitter release that particularly impact compartments dominated by CS+depression.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that IP3R knockdown caused adaptation in γ2 and γ3, which are compartments that show CS+ depression following aversive conditioning.

claims.claim: Blocking synaptic transmission from KCs inhibited the GRAB-ACh responses across compartments.
claims.source: Blocking synaptic transmission from KCs inhibited the GRAB-ACh responses across compartments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 3 shows statistically significant reductions in GRAB-ACh responses when Shibirets is activated at restrictive temperature.

claims.claim: R13F02-Gal4 labeled 745 ± 47 neurons out of ~2000 total KCs.
claims.source: To quantify the coverage of this driver, we counted GRAB-ACh labeled neurons (immunostained with an anti-GFP antibody), finding that R13F02-Gal4 labeled 745 ± 47 neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) out of ~2000 total KCs (Aso et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: Figure 4—figure supplement 3D,E shows cell counts from immunohistochemistry, and the total KC number is cited from Aso et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Inhibiting a relatively small subset of KCs significantly reduced the GRAB-ACh response from the MB compartments, demonstrating that KCs are the major ACh source.
claims.source: Inhibiting this relatively small subset of KCs significantly reduced the GRAB-ACh response from the MB compartments, demonstrating that KCs are the major ACh source, though cholinergic MBONs could also contribute to the signal (Scheffer et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the significant reduction in GRAB-ACh signal when only ~37% of KCs are blocked, with citation to Scheffer et al., 2020 regarding cholinergic MBONs.

claims.claim: The presynaptic plasticity observed in each compartment should be mirrored in the respective postsynaptic MBON(s) innervating that compartment.
claims.source: Since ACh release from each compartment provides input to unique postsynaptic MBONs, the presynaptic plasticity observed in each compartment should be mirrored in the respective postsynaptic MBON(s) innervating that compartment.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical organization where each compartment provides input to specific MBONs.

claims.claim: The γ2α′1 MBON exhibited an increase in the relative CS+ responses following appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: The γ2α′1 MBON exhibited an increase in the relative CS+ responses following conditioning (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Figure 5D shows a statistically significant difference between CS+ and CS- Δ(post/pre) values in the γ2α′1 MBON.

claims.claim: The γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs exhibited an increase in the relative CS+ responses following appetitive conditioning due to potentiation of the CS+ response.
claims.source: The γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs exhibited an increase in the relative CS+ responses (Figure 5F). In this case, it was due to potentiation of the CS+ response (Figure 5F).
claims.evidence: Figure 5F shows both a significant difference between CS+ and CS- and significant potentiation of CS+ compared to odor-only control.

claims.claim: The γ1pedc>α/β MBON exhibited a significant elevation of the CS+ response relative to the CS- following appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Following appetitive conditioning, the γ1pedc>α/β MBON exhibited a significant elevation of the CS+ response relative to the CS- (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C shows statistically significant differences in the γ1pedc>α/β MBON.

claims.claim: The elevation in CS+ response in the γ1pedc>α/β MBON was due to a potentiation of the CS+ response.
claims.source: This was due to a potentiation of the CS+ response, as the post-conditioning CS+ response was significantly larger than the corresponding odor-only control.
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C shows the CS+ Δ(post/pre) was significantly higher than the odor-only control.

claims.claim: Appetitive conditioning produced plasticity in the opposite direction in the γ5β′2 a MBON, with a decrease in the CS+ response relative to the CS-.
claims.source: Finally, appetitive conditioning produced plasticity in the opposite direction in the γ5β′2 a MBON; this neuron exhibited a decrease in the CS+ response relative to the CS- (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Figure 5—figure supplement 1E shows a statistically significant decrease in CS+ relative to CS- in the γ5β′2 a MBON.

claims.claim: The directionality of the plasticity in MBONs matched that observed in ACh responses in the presynaptic compartment.
claims.source: Overall, the directionality of the plasticity in MBONs matched that observed in ACh responses in the presynaptic compartment.
claims.evidence: This is concluded by comparing the patterns of plasticity in presynaptic ACh release (Figures 1-2) with postsynaptic MBON responses (Figure 5).

claims.claim: Compartmentalized, presynaptic plasticity in neurotransmitter release from the MB compartments likely plays a role in modulating the MBON responses following learning.
claims.source: Thus, compartmentalized, presynaptic plasticity in neurotransmitter release from the MB compartments likely plays a role in modulating the MBON responses following learning.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between presynaptic ACh plasticity and postsynaptic MBON plasticity patterns.

claims.claim: Blocking the γ2α′1 MBON did not significantly impair performance in appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: Blocking the γ2α′1 MBON did not significantly impair performance in appetitive conditioning (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows no statistically significant difference in performance index when γ2α′1 MBON is blocked compared to controls.

claims.claim: Blocking synaptic transmission from the γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs significantly impaired appetitive conditioning performance.
claims.source: In contrast, blocking synaptic transmission from the γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs significantly impaired appetitive conditioning performance (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Figure 5B shows a statistically significant reduction in performance index when γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs are blocked.

claims.claim: The output of the γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs serves a key role for normal appetitive short-term memory.
claims.source: This demonstrates that the output of the γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs is not only sufficient for protein synthesis-dependent appetitive long-term memory (Wu et al., 2017) but also serves a key role for normal appetitive short-term memory.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the behavioral impairment when γ3/γ3β′1 MBONs are blocked (Figure 5B), with citation to Wu et al., 2017 for long-term memory.

claims.claim: Compartmentalized plasticity in neurotransmitter release expands the potential computational capacity of learning circuits.
claims.source: Compartmentalized plasticity in neurotransmitter release expands the potential computational capacity of learning circuits.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claims.claim: Compartmentalized plasticity allows a set of odor-coding MB neurons to bifurcate their output to different downstream approach- and avoidance-driving output neurons.
claims.source: It allows a set of odor-coding MB neurons to bifurcate their output to different downstream approach- and avoidance-driving downstream output neurons, independently modulating the synaptic connections to alter action selection based on the conditioned value of olfactory stimuli.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that different compartments of the same KCs show different patterns of plasticity that connect to MBONs with different behavioral valences.

claims.claim: The KCs modify the encoded value of olfactory stimuli through bidirectional plasticity in odor responses, which vary in a compartment-specific manner along the length of the axons.
claims.source: The KCs modify the encoded value of olfactory stimuli through bidirectional plasticity in odor responses, which vary in a compartment-specific manner along the length of the axons.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data showing different patterns of potentiation and depression across compartments (Figures 1-2).

claims.claim: Learning-induced plasticity of ACh release in the MB was bidirectional within the compartment, depending on the valence of the US.
claims.source: Learning-induced plasticity of ACh release in the MB was bidirectional within the compartment, depending on the valence of the US, and was coherent with the valence of the MBON downstream of the compartment.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from comparing appetitive (Figure 1) and aversive (Figure 2) conditioning effects in the same compartments.

claims.claim: The γ2 and γ3 MB compartments exhibited plasticity that was coherent with promoting behavioral approach following appetitive conditioning and avoidance after aversive conditioning.
claims.source: Notably, the γ2 and γ3 MB compartments, which relay information to approach-promoting MBONs (Aso et al., 2014b), exhibited plasticity that was coherent with promoting behavioral approach following appetitive conditioning and avoidance after aversive conditioning.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the opposite patterns of plasticity in γ2 and γ3 following appetitive versus aversive conditioning, with citation to Aso et al., 2014b for MBON valence.

claims.claim: Aversive conditioning was previously reported to decrease neurotransmitter release from KCs.
claims.source: Aversive conditioning was previously reported to decrease neurotransmitter release from KCs (Zhang and Roman, 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Pairing odor with stimulation of appetitive PAM dopaminergic neurons potentiates odor-evoked cytosolic Ca2+ transients across the KC compartments.
claims.source: Pairing odor with stimulation of appetitive PAM dopaminergic neurons potentiates odor-evoked cytosolic Ca2+ transients across the KC compartments (Boto et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Boto et al., 2014.

claims.claim: Appetitive conditioning increases odor-evoked Ca2+ transients across KC compartments.
claims.source: Appetitive conditioning increases odor-evoked Ca2+ transients across KC compartments (Louis et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Louis et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Stimulation of dopaminergic circuits associated with reward learning potentiate MB γ4 connections with the respective γ4 MBON.
claims.source: Stimulation of dopaminergic circuits associated with reward learning potentiate MB γ4 connections with the respective γ4 MBON (Handler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Handler et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Classical conditioning produces no compartmentalized differences in odor-evoked Ca2+ responses in KCs.
claims.source: In contrast, classical conditioning produces no compartmentalized differences in odor-evoked Ca2+ responses.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a contrast to other findings, drawing on prior literature.

claims.claim: Appetitive conditioning with odor + sucrose pairing increases odor-evoked cytosolic Ca2+ transients in KCs across the γ lobe compartments.
claims.source: Appetitive conditioning with odor + sucrose pairing increases odor-evoked cytosolic Ca2+ transients in KCs across the γ lobe compartments (Louis et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Louis et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Aversive conditioning produces no net change in Ca2+ responses across the KC compartments.
claims.source: Aversive conditioning produces no net change across the compartments (Louis et al., 2018), but alters synapse-specific Ca2+ responses at the individual bouton level (Bilz et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Louis et al., 2018 and Bilz et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Learning drives compartmentalized plasticity in neurotransmitter release that is coherent with the behavioral valence of the corresponding MBON.
claims.source: A major conclusion of the present study is that learning drives compartmentalized plasticity in neurotransmitter release that is coherent with the behavioral valence of the corresponding MBON.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a major conclusion, supported by the experimental data showing correlation between presynaptic ACh plasticity and MBON valence.

claims.claim: CaV2 channels regulate several forms of synaptic plasticity, including paired-pulse facilitation, homeostatic plasticity, and long-term potentiation.
claims.source: CaV2 channels regulate several forms of synaptic plasticity, including paired-pulse facilitation, homeostatic plasticity, and long-term potentiation (Frank et al., 2006; Inchauspe et al., 2004; Nanou et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Cac underlies potentiation but not depression of learning-induced plasticity in the MB.
claims.source: Our data suggest that these channels regulate the spatial patterns of learning-induced plasticity in the MB unidirectionally (from baseline), with Cac underlying potentiation but not depression.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the observation that Cac knockdown eliminated potentiation (Figure 3) but not depression (Figure 4).

claims.claim: CaV2 channel activity is modulated by presynaptic calcium and G protein-coupled receptor activity.
claims.source: CaV2 channel activity is modulated by presynaptic calcium and G protein-coupled receptor activity (Zamponi and Currie, 2013), and channel localization in the active zone dynamically regulates synaptic strength (Gratz et al., 2019; Lübbert et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Cac insertion into, or increased clustering within, the active zones may underlie learning-induced potentiation.
claims.source: Thus, Cac insertion into, or increased clustering within, the active zones may underlie learning-induced potentiation (e.g. in the γ1-γ2 compartments following appetitive conditioning).
claims.evidence: This is speculated based on known mechanisms of CaV2 channel regulation and the observed requirement for Cac in potentiation.

claims.claim: IP3R was necessary to maintain normal odor responsivity when odors were presented repeatedly across multiple trials.
claims.source: In contrast to the Cac effect on potentiation, IP3R was necessary to maintain normal odor responsivity when odors were presented repeatedly across multiple trials (whether those were pre/post trials in the conditioning protocol or 10× odor presentations in the adaptation protocol).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the adaptation observed in IP3R knockdown animals across repeated odor presentations (Figure 4).

claims.claim: The temporal role of IP3R in maintenance of presynaptic homeostatic potentiation at the neuromuscular junction is broadly consistent with its role in maintaining odor responsivity in KCs.
claims.source: This is broadly consistent with the temporal role of IP3R in maintenance of presynaptic homeostatic potentiation at the neuromuscular junction (James et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim draws a parallel to prior work, supported by citation to James et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Dopaminergic circuits associated with reward learning drive release of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum when activated with KCs in a backward pairing paradigm ex vivo.
claims.source: In addition, dopaminergic circuits associated with reward learning drive release of Ca2+ from the endoplasmic reticulum when activated with KCs in a backward pairing paradigm ex vivo, potentiating MB γ4 connections with the respective γ4 MBON (Handler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Handler et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Potentiation and depression of ACh release were observed across multiple MB compartments following conditioning.
claims.source: We observed potentiation and depression of ACh release across multiple MB compartments following conditioning, providing a presynaptic mechanism that potentially contributes to shaping conditioned MBON responses.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the experimental data in Figures 1 and 2 showing both potentiation and depression in different compartments.

claims.claim: By comparing the CS+ and CS- responses to those of untrained odors, plasticity was ascribed to potentiation or depression, accounting for any non-associative olfactory adaptation.
claims.source: Importantly, by comparing the CS+ and CS- responses to those of untrained odors, we ascribed plasticity to potentiation or depression (accounting for any non-associative olfactory adaptation) within each compartment.
claims.evidence: This describes the methodological approach used throughout the study to distinguish associative plasticity from adaptation.

claims.claim: A gradient of CS+ potentiation to CS- depression was observed following appetitive conditioning in the γ1–γ3 compartments.
claims.source: Specifically, the CS+/CS- relationship changed in a linear gradient down the γ1–γ3 compartments following appetitive conditioning. Appetitive conditioning increased CS+ responses in the γ1 compartment, while decreasing the CS- responses in the γ3 compartment. The γ2 compartment yielded a mix of these responses.
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 1 showing CS+ potentiation in γ1, both CS+ potentiation and CS- depression in γ2, and CS- depression trend in γ3.

claims.claim: The patterns of plasticity have the net effect of increasing the relative response to the CS+ odor, which would bias the animal to approach the CS+.
claims.source: These patterns of plasticity have the net effect of increasing the relative response to the CS+ odor (↑CS+:CS-). Since the MBONs postsynaptic to these compartments drive behavioral approach (Aso et al., 2014b), this would bias the animal to approach the CS+ if it encountered both odors simultaneously.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the increased CS+:CS- ratio in approach-promoting compartments, with citation to Aso et al., 2014b for MBON behavioral effects.

claims.claim: The CS+ and CS- produce different patterns of plasticity at different loci, which presumably coordinate to regulate behavior via temporal integration of the odor and US cues.
claims.source: The CS+ and CS- produce different patterns of plasticity at different loci (e.g. γ1 vs γ3), which presumably coordinate to regulate behavior via temporal integration of the odor and US cues (Berry et al., 2018; Handler et al., 2019; Jacob and Waddell, 2020; König et al., 2018; Tanimoto et al., 2004; Tully and Quinn, 1985).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the spatial patterns of plasticity, with supporting citations to prior literature on temporal integration in learning.

claims.claim: The γ5 compartment exhibited plasticity in the opposite direction from γ1–γ3, decreasing the relative response to the CS+ odor following appetitive conditioning.
claims.source: For instance, while the γ1–γ3 compartments exhibited ↑CS+:CS- following appetitive conditioning, the γ5 compartment exhibited plasticity in the opposite direction: decreasing the relative response to the CS+ odor (↓CS+:CS-).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from the data in Figure 1 showing opposite patterns of plasticity in γ5 compared to γ1-γ3.

claims.claim: The γ5 compartment is presynaptic to an avoidance-promoting MBON.
claims.source: As the γ5 compartment is presynaptic to an avoidance-promoting MBON, this plasticity pattern would coherently contribute to biasing the animal toward CS+ approach (reducing CS+ avoidance).

results.result: Appetitive conditioning produces compartmentalized, bidirectional plasticity of acetylcholine release across mushroom body γ lobe compartments, with a proximal-to-distal gradient from CS+ potentiation (γ1) to CS- depression (γ3), and opposite plasticity in the distal γ5 compartment.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C20 provide converging experimental evidence from GRAB-ACh imaging (Figure 1) showing statistically significant, compartment-specific patterns of ACh release plasticity following appetitive conditioning. The data demonstrate CS+ potentiation in γ1, both CS+ potentiation and CS- depression in γ2, CS- depression trends in γ3, and reduced CS+:CS- in γ5, with appropriate odor-only controls to distinguish associative plasticity from adaptation.

results.result: Aversive conditioning produces plasticity in the opposite direction from appetitive conditioning in the same compartments (γ2 and γ3), demonstrating valence-dependent bidirectional plasticity that is coherent with downstream MBON behavioral valence.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by experimental data (Figure 2) showing CS+ depression in γ2 and γ3 following aversive conditioning, which is opposite to the pattern observed with appetitive conditioning in the same compartments. This bidirectional plasticity depending on US valence is a key finding, though the mechanism linking presynaptic plasticity to MBON valence is inferred rather than directly demonstrated.

results.result: Potentiation of acetylcholine release following appetitive conditioning requires the CaV2.1 calcium channel cacophony, while depression does not, demonstrating distinct molecular mechanisms for bidirectional plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 are supported by conditional RNAi experiments (Figure 3) showing that ~29% Cac knockdown eliminates CS+ potentiation across γ1-γ3 while preserving baseline ACh release and CS+ depression trends in γ5. However, the moderate knockdown level (29%) raises questions about whether complete elimination would reveal additional roles, and the persistence of depression could reflect compensation or distinct mechanisms.

results.result: Moderate knockdown of cacophony does not impair learning-induced depression of ACh release following aversive conditioning.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are supported by data (Figure 4A-F) showing that Cac knockdown preserves CS+ depression in γ2 following aversive conditioning, with trends in other compartments matching controls. This supports the conclusion that potentiation and depression rely on distinct mechanisms, though the moderate knockdown level limits strong conclusions about Cac's role in depression.

results.result: Conditional cacophony knockdown impairs behavioral appetitive conditioning performance without affecting odor acuity, suggesting that learning-induced facilitation of neurotransmitter release contributes to reward learning behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by behavioral data (Figure 3H) showing significant impairment in appetitive conditioning with Cac knockdown, while odor avoidance remains intact (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B). The link between impaired CS+ potentiation and behavioral deficit is correlative rather than causally demonstrated, but the convergence of physiological and behavioral phenotypes provides strong support.

results.result: The inositol triphosphate receptor (IP3R) is required to maintain odor responsivity upon repeated presentations and to preserve post-conditioning contrast between CS+ and CS-, preventing adaptation particularly in compartments dominated by CS+ depression.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 and C53-C54 are supported by IP3R knockdown experiments (Figure 4) showing loss of CS+/CS- contrast due to adaptation in CS- and odor-only controls rather than loss of CS+ depression. The adaptation assay (Figure 4J-L) directly demonstrates that IP3R knockdown causes significant adaptation in γ2 and γ3 across repeated odor presentations, while controls show no adaptation. This provides strong mechanistic evidence for IP3R's role in maintaining synaptic responsivity.

results.result: IP3R knockdown produces compartment-specific olfactory adaptation, with significant effects in γ2 and γ3 but not in γ1, γ4, or γ5.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C52 are supported by the adaptation protocol data (Figure 4K-L, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing statistically significant decreases in ACh release across repeated odor presentations in γ2 and γ3 with IP3R knockdown, while controls show no adaptation. The compartment-specific effects suggest regional differences in IP3R function or expression, though the mechanism underlying this spatial specificity is not explored.

results.result: Kenyon cells are the major source of acetylcholine signals detected by GRAB-ACh, as demonstrated by Shibirets blockade experiments showing that inhibiting ~37% of KCs significantly reduces GRAB-ACh responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by control experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) showing significant reduction in GRAB-ACh signals when KC synaptic transmission is blocked, with cell counts confirming R13F02-Gal4 labels 745±47 neurons (~37% of total KCs). However, the residual signal and potential contribution from cholinergic MBONs (acknowledged by authors) introduces some uncertainty about signal source attribution.

results.result: Compartmentalized presynaptic plasticity in ACh release correlates with postsynaptic changes in MBONs, with the directionality of plasticity matching between presynaptic compartments and their corresponding postsynaptic MBONs.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C64 are supported by Ca2+ imaging in MBONs (Figure 5) showing plasticity patterns that match the directionality observed in presynaptic ACh release: γ2α'1 and γ3/γ3β'1 MBONs show increased CS+ responses, γ1pedc>α/β shows CS+ potentiation, and γ5β'2a shows decreased CS+ responses. However, the correlation is not perfect (e.g., γ3 presynaptic shows CS- depression but γ3 MBON shows CS+ potentiation), and the causal link is inferred rather than directly tested.

results.result: The γ3/γ3β'1 MBONs are required for normal appetitive short-term memory, while the γ2α'1 MBON is not, suggesting specific roles for different approach-promoting MBONs in reward learning.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by behavioral experiments (Figure 5B) showing significant impairment in appetitive conditioning when γ3/γ3β'1 MBONs are blocked with Shibirets, while blocking γ2α'1 MBON has no significant effect. This demonstrates functional specificity among approach-promoting MBONs, though the mechanism underlying this differential requirement is not explored.

results.result: Learning drives compartmentalized, bidirectional plasticity of synaptic neurotransmitter release that relies on distinct molecular mechanisms (Cac for potentiation, IP3R for maintaining responsivity), expanding the computational capacity of learning circuits by allowing independent modulation of axonal compartments.
results.evaluation: This overarching conclusion integrates multiple lines of evidence showing bidirectional plasticity (Figures 1-2), distinct molecular mechanisms (Figures 3-4), and correlation with MBON responses (Figure 5). The claim about expanding computational capacity is supported by the demonstration of compartment-specific, valence-dependent plasticity, though the actual computational consequences are inferred rather than directly measured.

results.result: The spatial gradient of plasticity across compartments (CS+ potentiation in γ1 to CS- depression in γ3) has the net effect of increasing relative CS+ responses in approach-promoting compartments, which would bias the animal toward CS+ approach behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by the experimental design using odor-only controls to distinguish associative plasticity from adaptation, and by the observed gradient of plasticity across γ1-γ3. The behavioral interpretation (C92) is logical given the known valence of downstream MBONs (cited from Aso et al., 2014b), though the direct causal link between the plasticity gradient and approach behavior is not experimentally tested.

results.result: Redundancy and/or different weighting across approach-promoting MBONs renders the system resilient to silencing individual MBONs, with different MBONs having differing roles across time in appetitive memory processing.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are supported by the differential behavioral effects of blocking γ2α'1 versus γ3/γ3β'1 MBONs (Figure 5B) and comparison with prior work (Ichinose et al., 2021). The inference about redundancy is reasonable given the lack of impairment when γ2α'1 is blocked despite its approach-promoting valence, though alternative explanations (e.g., differential weighting) are not distinguished.

results.result: Axonal compartmentalization may enable localized, presynaptic plasticity to alter neuronal output in a flexible, experience-dependent manner, increasing the computational capacity of circuits.
results.evaluation: Claim C11 is stated as general knowledge without specific citation in the manuscript, but is well-established in the literature. Claim C12 is presented as a hypothesis that is then tested and supported by the experimental data throughout the manuscript showing compartment-specific plasticity. The hypothesis is well-supported by the results.

results.result: Prior studies documented primarily depression at KC-MBON synapses following conditioning, with compartmentalized Ca2+ effects observed in some contexts but not classical conditioning protocols.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C22 and C74-C80 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for the current findings showing bidirectional plasticity, which extends beyond the primarily depression-focused prior work. The citations appear accurate and relevant.

results.result: CaV2 channels and IP3R-mediated ER Ca2+ release are major sources of stimulus-evoked intracellular Ca2+ that regulate various forms of synaptic plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C28, C42, C82, and C84 accurately summarize established knowledge from prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide necessary background for interpreting the Cac and IP3R knockdown experiments. The citations appear accurate and relevant.

results.result: Cac insertion/clustering in active zones may underlie learning-induced potentiation, and IP3R's role in maintaining odor responsivity is consistent with its role in presynaptic homeostatic potentiation at the neuromuscular junction.
results.evaluation: Claim C85 is explicitly speculative, proposing a mechanism for Cac-dependent potentiation based on known CaV2 channel regulation but without direct experimental evidence. Claim C87 draws a parallel to prior work (James et al., 2019) which is reasonable but not directly tested. These mechanistic proposals are plausible but require additional experiments for validation.

results.result: Alterations in MBON activity following learning result from multiple mechanisms including presynaptic and postsynaptic plasticity, feedforward inhibition, and distributed plasticity across multiple circuit nodes, with plasticity guiding behavior through probabilistic biasing of network activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C109 synthesize current findings with prior literature (with appropriate citations) to provide a comprehensive model of how plasticity is distributed across the learning circuit. The integration of presynaptic plasticity (current work) with known postsynaptic mechanisms and circuit-level effects (prior work) is well-supported, though the specific claim about probabilistic biasing (C109) is more speculative.
